planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in cool, well-drained soil, and provide afternoon shade in hot lowland climates it is not adapted to.

directions: Subalpine fir is the slender, spire-like conifer behind the compact blue-needled dwarf garden cultivars already grown, forming a narrow silhouette adapted to shedding heavy mountain snow loads in its native high-elevation range. Its soft, blue-green needles and tight branching give it an elegant, formal appearance even as a full-sized tree. Plant in full sun to light shade on cool, moist, well-drained soil, since it struggles in hot, humid, or compacted lowland conditions far from its native subalpine habitat. It is best suited to cooler northern or high-elevation gardens rather than hot summer climates.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into moist, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade, sheltered from strong wind.

directions: Full moon maple is the Japanese wild-type species behind the finely cut, vine-leaf named selections already grown, bearing broad, rounded, many-lobed leaves that turn a spectacular blend of orange, red, and purple in fall. Compared to the more familiar Japanese maple, it carries larger, softer-textured leaves and a slightly more upright, less delicate habit. Plant in partial shade on moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and the hottest afternoon sun. It is a reliable large shrub or small specimen tree for a woodland garden edge, needing little pruning beyond removing damaged wood.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Shirasawa's Maple (Golden Full Moon Maple, Wild-Type Species)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into moist, well-drained soil in dappled shade, protected from hot afternoon sun and wind.

directions: Shirasawa's maple is the Japanese wild-type species behind the popular golden-leaved 'Aureum' and coral-bark named selections already grown, bearing rounded, finely toothed leaves on a graceful, broadly rounded small tree. It shares the refined, layered branching of Japanese maple but with a slightly bolder leaf texture, and colors richly in fall. Plant in dappled shade on moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, since strong sun and drying wind can scorch the leaves, especially on lighter-colored selections. It makes an excellent specimen or understory tree in a shaded garden bed.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Direct sow or set divisions around last frost into moist, well-drained soil; it tolerates more moisture than most yarrows.

directions: Sneezewort is the European wild-type species behind the double white pompon selections such as 'The Pearl,' bearing clusters of small, simple white daisy flowers on an upright, spreading perennial. Unlike most border yarrows, it tolerates consistently moist soil and light shade without declining, making it useful in damper border situations other Achillea species dislike. Plant in full sun to light shade on moist, well-drained soil, and divide every few years to keep the spreading clumps in check. Deadheading extends the midsummer bloom season and helps curb its tendency to self-sow.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, and give it room to mature into a substantial clump.

directions: Japanese bugbane is the species behind the purple-stemmed named selections such as 'Elstead,' sending up tall, airy spikes of small white, fragrant flowers above handsome, deeply cut dark foliage in late summer and fall. It is one of the latest-blooming shade perennials, extending interest in a woodland border well past the main summer flush. Plant in partial to full shade on consistently moist, humus-rich soil, and shelter it from strong wind, which can topple the tall flower spikes. It is long-lived and slow to spread, rewarding patience with an increasingly substantial clump over the years.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

subcategory: perennial border and rock garden flower

planting.note: Direct sow or set divisions around last frost into well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: False sea thrift is the Portuguese wild-type species behind the larger-flowered Dreameria-series named selections already grown, carrying round, globe-like flower heads on taller, sturdier stems than common sea thrift. It forms a neat basal rosette of broad, strap-shaped leaves and blooms over a long season from late spring into summer. Plant in full sun on well-drained, even sandy soil, since it is intolerant of heavy, wet ground. Established plants are drought tolerant and need only the occasional removal of spent flower stems to look tidy.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into rich, moist, well-drained woodland soil in shade, with winter protection in the colder part of its range.

directions: Panda face ginger is the Chinese wild-type species famous for its unusual black-and-white mottled flowers hidden at soil level beneath heart-shaped evergreen leaves, a pattern that gave rise to its whimsical common name and the named selections such as 'Ling Ling' already grown. Collectors part the foliage each spring to find the curious bicolor blooms tucked beneath the leaf canopy. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade, with protection from harsh winter exposure at the colder end of its range. It spreads slowly into a low, dense colony and resents root disturbance once settled in.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, watering regularly the first season.

directions: This New Zealand sedge is the wild-type species behind the popular bronze-toned named selections such as 'Toffee Twist,' forming an arching, fountain-like mound of fine, wiry, warm brown to olive-green leaves. It provides excellent fine-textured contrast against broader-leaved perennials in a border or container planting. Plant in full sun to light shade on well-drained soil, providing afternoon shade and consistent moisture in hot inland climates. It is evergreen in mild climates and benefits from an occasional combing out of old leaves to keep its texture fresh.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade.

directions: Palm sedge is the East Asian wild-type species behind the variegated 'Sparkler' and 'Spark Plug' named selections already grown, carrying unusually broad, whorled leaves radiating from the stem tips in a pattern resembling a miniature palm frond. The plain green form shares the same architectural, tropical-looking silhouette that makes this sedge distinctive among ornamental Carex. Plant in partial shade on moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, and protect it from hard freezes at the colder end of its hardiness range. It makes a striking textural accent in a shaded border or large container.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring into moist, well-drained soil with room for its eventual large, often weeping form.

directions: Nootka cypress, also called Alaska cedar, is the Pacific Northwest wild-type conifer behind the popular weeping named garden selections already grown, forming a tall, often irregular tree with drooping branch tips and scaly, blue-green foliage. In the wild it grows at higher elevations and in cooler, wetter climates than most garden cypress, and it carries that same preference for cool roots and consistent moisture into cultivation. Plant in full sun to light shade on moist, well-drained soil, avoiding hot, dry inland sites where it struggles. It is slow-growing but long-lived, eventually forming an imposing, picturesque specimen tree.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; unlike most heaths it tolerates slightly alkaline conditions as well.

directions: Winter heath is the European wild-type species behind the many named ground-covering cultivars already grown for their late-winter color, bearing small, urn-shaped pink to white flowers that open even through light snow cover. It forms a low, dense evergreen mat of fine needle-like foliage that spreads to knit together a weed-suppressing carpet over a few seasons. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; it is one of the few heaths that tolerates slightly alkaline ground in addition to the acidic soil most Erica species demand. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and compact.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; this stable garden hybrid tolerates slightly alkaline conditions better than most heaths.

directions: Darley heath is a long-stable garden hybrid between winter heath and Irish heath, combining the long winter-into-spring bloom season of the former with a slightly larger, more vigorous habit from the latter. Plain seedlings bear small bell-shaped pink to white flowers over a low, dense evergreen mound, the same base form behind named selections like 'Kramer's Rote' and 'Silberschmelze' already grown. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, where it tolerates both acidic and mildly alkaline conditions better than most true heath species. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain a tight, mounded shape.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, since the taprooted seedlings resent being transplanted later.

directions: Pyrenean sea holly is the Spanish and French mountain wild-type species behind the silver-veined named selections such as 'Oxford Blue,' bearing spiny, marbled gray-green leaves and steel-blue thistle-like flower heads in summer. It thrives in the same lean, rocky, well-drained conditions found on its native Pyrenean slopes. Plant in full sun on sharply drained soil, since rich or consistently moist ground causes it to rot. Once its deep taproot is established it is drought tolerant and long-lived, best left undisturbed rather than divided or moved.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Seed in early fall for the best establishment, or in early spring as a second choice, into well-prepared soil.

directions: Tall fescue is the deep-rooted, cool-season turf and forage grass species behind the variegated and dwarf ornamental selections already grown, forming a coarse but durable bunchgrass sod widely used on lawns, pastures, and roadsides across the transition zone. Its deep root system makes it notably more drought and heat tolerant than other cool-season turf grasses, allowing it to hold up through summer stress that would thin out bluegrass. Sow seed in early fall for best establishment, or in early spring as a second choice, into well-prepared soil in full sun to light shade. Mow at a height of three inches or more to encourage deep rooting and shade out weeds.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in a well-drained, chunky potting mix, and keep warm and humid until roots establish.

directions: Hoya krohniana is the Indonesian wild-type species behind the variegated 'Eskimo' and 'Silver Splash' named selections already grown, carrying thick, quilted, deep green leaves on a slow-growing vine prized for its foliage more than its small, inconspicuous flower clusters. It prefers bright, indirect light and a chunky, fast-draining potting mix similar to other wax plants, letting the soil dry somewhat between waterings. Pot in a well-drained orchid-style mix and keep temperatures above 55 degrees Fahrenheit year-round, since it has no frost tolerance. Provide a small trellis or allow it to trail from a hanging basket to show off its distinctive puckered foliage.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Taiwan ixora is the compact East Asian wild-type species behind the popular dwarf red and yellow named selections already grown as low flowering hedges and foundation shrubs. It produces dense, rounded clusters of small star-shaped flowers almost continuously through the warm season in frost-free climates. Plant in full sun to partial shade on well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and protect it from frost, since it has little cold tolerance. Light, regular feeding and consistent moisture keep the naturally compact shrub flowering heavily with minimal pruning.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; the species grows larger and more mounded than the familiar 'Nana' dwarf form.

directions: Japanese garden juniper is the wild-type species behind the dwarf, mat-forming 'Nana' selection that is far more commonly planted than the species itself, carrying the same dense, prickly blue-green scale-like foliage on a somewhat larger, more mounded groundcover shrub. It spreads steadily across banks, rock gardens, and dry slopes, rooting where branches touch soil. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, where it is highly drought tolerant and resistant to most pest problems once established. It needs no fertilizer and only occasional trimming to keep it within bounds.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun, giving it room to grow into a substantial, cinnamon-barked tree.

directions: Japanese crape myrtle is the mildew-resistant species used as the breeding parent behind nearly every modern disease-resistant crape myrtle hybrid already grown, such as the National Arboretum's Indian-tribe-named series. The species itself is prized in its own right for exceptionally showy, exfoliating cinnamon-colored bark and pure white summer flower clusters on a vigorous, fast-growing tree. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, and give it considerably more room than typical crape myrtle cultivars, since the straight species grows into a much larger tree. It is naturally resistant to powdery mildew, the main disease problem of common crape myrtle.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; choose a sterile or variegated named selection where fruiting privet has become an invasive concern, since the wild species seeds prolifically by bird-dispersed berries.

directions: Chinese privet is the fast-growing wild-type species behind the golden-leaved 'Sunshine' and variegated 'Jack Frost' named selections already grown as low-fruit or non-flowering hedge plants. The unselected species flowers profusely and sets abundant small black berries that birds spread widely, and it has become a serious invasive woodland shrub across much of the southeastern United States, so gardeners should generally favor a named non-fruiting or sterile selection over the straight species. Where grown, plant in full sun to partial shade on well-drained soil, and shear regularly to maintain a formal hedge. Because of its invasive potential, avoid planting the unselected species near wild areas or waterways.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after frost danger passes into moist, well-drained soil or a hanging basket.

directions: This Chinese wild-type species is the parent behind the variegated 'Outback Sunset' and other named trailing selections already grown in hanging baskets and as groundcover, bearing clustered, bright yellow flowers along trailing stems lined with rounded green leaves. It spreads quickly as a groundcover in mild climates or trails attractively from a container in colder zones where it is grown as an annual. Plant in full sun to partial shade on consistently moist, well-drained soil, and pinch back stem tips to encourage denser, bushier growth. It roots readily wherever stems touch soil, making propagation easy.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun, protecting young trees from hard freezes in the cooler end of its range.

directions: Himalayan long mulberry is the Asian wild-type species behind the giant, extra-long named selections such as 'Pakistan' and 'Saharanpur' already grown for their remarkably elongated, sweet fruit. The species produces notably longer fruit clusters than common mulberry, sometimes reaching several inches, with a mild, honeyed flavor best eaten fresh since the fruit bruises easily. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, and protect young trees through their first winters in the cooler parts of its hardiness range. Once established it is a vigorous, fast-growing tree needing little more than occasional pruning to control size.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well after the last frost; this warm-season grass germinates poorly in cool soil.

directions: Kleingrass is the drought-tolerant South African wild-type species behind the named forage selections such as 'Selection 75' and 'Verde' already used for grazing and hay across the southern Plains and Texas. It is a tough, rhizomatous perennial bunchgrass well suited to heat and extended dry spells once established, though it is only lightly to moderately palatable compared with some other warm-season forages. Direct sow into warm soil in full sun, and allow a full season of establishment before grazing or heavy cutting. It tolerates poor, low-fertility soils and requires minimal input once a stand is established.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, protecting from frost.

directions: Garlic passionflower is the Brazilian wild-type species behind the named compact and large-flowered selections such as 'Corupa' and 'Iporanga' already grown by collectors, named for the distinct garlic-like scent released when its leaves are crushed. It bears showy red flowers followed by edible yellow-orange fruit, climbing readily on a trellis or fence in frost-free gardens. Plant in full sun to partial shade on well-drained, fertile soil, and protect it from frost, since it has very limited cold tolerance. Regular feeding and consistent moisture during the growing season support the best flowering and fruit set.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Mountain flax is the New Zealand wild-type species behind the colorful variegated named selections such as 'Jester' and 'Yellow Wave' already grown, forming an arching, strap-leaved fountain of foliage that stays smaller and more lax than its upright relative New Zealand flax. In its plain form the leaves are a solid green, but the architectural, fan-shaped habit that makes the named cultivars so popular is already fully present in the species. Plant in full sun to light shade on well-drained soil, and provide winter protection or grow in a container at the colder end of its hardiness range. It makes a striking accent in a border or large container with minimal ongoing care.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this pioneer pine thrives on poor ground that would stunt other conifers.

directions: Jack pine is the tough, cold-hardy North American species behind the dwarf and weeping named selections such as 'Uncle Fogy' and 'Schoodic' already grown, a scrubby, twisted-needled pioneer tree adapted to the poorest, sandiest soils and the coldest climates of any North American pine. Its irregular, often picturesque branching and tolerance of drought, wind, and nutrient-poor ground make it a tough choice for difficult northern sites. Plant in full sun on lean, well-drained soil, and avoid rich or consistently moist ground, which it does not need and does not tolerate as well as poor soil. It needs essentially no fertilizing or supplemental watering once established.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun, giving it room for its eventual dense pyramidal form.

directions: Bosnian pine is the Balkan mountain species behind the dwarf named selections such as 'Compact Gem' and 'Smidtii' already grown, forming a dense, tidy pyramid of dark green needles that holds its shape without much pruning. It is unusually tolerant of urban pollution, heat, drought, and alkaline soil compared with many other pines, making it a reliable choice well outside its native mountain range. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil of almost any pH, and expect slow but steady growth into a handsome, formally shaped specimen tree. It needs very little maintenance once established.

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun, giving it generous room for its mature, often irregular form.

directions: Scots pine is the widespread Eurasian species behind the low, spreading 'Hillside Creeper' and dwarf 'Watereri' named selections already grown, a fast-growing forest and landscape tree known for its distinctive orange-flaking upper bark and irregular, often flat-topped crown with age. It is extremely adaptable, tolerating poor sandy soils, cold, drought, and wind better than most ornamental conifers. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil of almost any type, and allow plenty of room, since the mature tree can become quite large and broad. It is also widely grown as a classic Christmas tree species in plantations across the eastern United States.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring into sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun.

directions: Globe-headed hens and chicks is a Central European wild-type species that, in its hairy subsp. hirtum form, is the parent behind the spiky-leaved named selections such as 'Hedgehog' already grown by succulent collectors. True to its Sempervivum habit, the compact rosette sends out short runners tipped with small globe-shaped offset rosettes rather than the long stolons seen in common hens and chicks. Plant in full sun on sharply drained, mineral-rich soil, such as a scree bed, trough, or rock garden crevice. It is cold hardy and drought tolerant once established, needing only occasional division to prevent overcrowding.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun, giving it room to grow into a vase-shaped shade tree.

directions: David's elm is the East Asian wild-type species that, through its Japanese botanical variety, parented widely planted disease-resistant hybrid shade trees like 'Accolade' and 'Discovery' already grown as Dutch elm disease-resistant replacements for American elm. The species itself shares that same strong resistance and a graceful, vase-shaped to rounded crown with attractive mottled bark on older specimens. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, where it tolerates urban conditions and a range of soil types well. It is fast-growing for an elm and needs only routine structural pruning while young to develop a strong branch framework.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring on a sturdy arbor or pergola in well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Silky wisteria is the Japanese wild-type species behind the named selections such as 'Shiro-Kapitan' and 'Showa-Beni' already grown, distinguished from the more commonly planted Japanese and Chinese wisterias by shorter, denser flower clusters and leaves with a soft, silky hairiness on the undersides. It is somewhat less aggressive and easier to manage on a garden structure than its more rampant relatives, while still producing a generous spring flush of fragrant blooms. Plant on a sturdy arbor, pergola, or trellis in full sun on well-drained soil, and prune after flowering to control size and encourage next year's bloom. Like other wisterias it can take several years to reach flowering maturity from a young plant.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
